figures.label: Figure 1
figures.caption: The two branches of IndexMem++: evict and recovery both inside one softmax.
figures.headline: The selection and recovery branches of IndexMem++ both read through one softmax, so evicting and restoring share the same normalizer.
citing_sentences: We instantiate these findings in IndexMem++, which follows a two-branch design (Yang et al., 2026), summarized in Figure 1: a selection branch evicts redundant KV entries, and a recovery branch summarizes what was evicted, both reading through one softmax.
Section 3 explains why this makes direct training fail, how to train a useful ranking, and how the recovery branch of Figure 1 restores part of the discarded contribution through the same normalizer.

figures.label: Figure 2
figures.caption: Differentiable gates can act at different points in attention. (a) Gates on queries, keys, values, or outputs; (b) an additive logit bias; (c) a gate on the value branch; (d) a multiplicative logit scale; and (e) a modification of the denominator alone. All keep the gate in the computation graph, but they have different effects on attention mass. A value gate suppresses a contribution without renormalizing the other weights, whereas a per-key logit bias $\log g_{j}$ redistributes mass and recovers attention over the retained set in the binary limit.
figures.headline: Only the per-key additive logit bias redistributes mass to the remaining entries, while value gates leave the other weights unchanged.

figures.label: Figure 3
figures.caption: Scorer architectures. All variants map $x_{j}=\operatorname{Norm}(h_{j})$ to per-head retention scores and differ only in what they read besides $x_{j}$. (a) A linear readout and (b) the token-local MLP used as the reference scorer see the current hidden state alone. The three history variants add one branch that is summed into the MLP’s pre-activation: (c) a depthwise causal convolution over the previous eight tokens, (d) a gated recurrence carrying a fixed-size state $S_{j-1}$, and (e) a single-head causal attention over the prefix up to $j$. The added branch is initialized to zero, so each variant starts exactly from (b).
figures.headline: Five scorer variants differ only in what history they read beside the current hidden state, starting from a token-local MLP.
citing_sentences: We next study the scorer architectures in Figure 3.
Figure 3 shows the five scorers side by side, including the linear readout and the token-local MLP used as references.

figures.label: Figure 4
figures.caption: Recovery architectures. Linear-state and TTT memories add recovery after attention; centroid KV competes with retained entries within the same softmax.
figures.headline: Linear-state and TTT memories add recovery after attention, while centroid KV competes with retained entries inside the same softmax.
citing_sentences: We test a linear associative state $W:k\mapsto v$ and a TTT-style MLP fitted to the evicted pairs at inference, both read afterwards as $\alpha(q)o_{S}+\beta(q)m_{E}(q)$ (Figure 4).
Figure 4 contrasts this readout with the output-space memories above.

figures.label: Figure 5
figures.caption: Decode throughput versus input length for Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B. Full-KV* is the Full-KV reference measured under the protocol of Appendix D.
figures.headline: IndexMem++ decode throughput declines modestly with input length, while Full-KV points are missing where runs ran out of memory.
citing_sentences: Figure 5 reports batch throughput for 256 decode steps on a single H20 GPU at an average per-KV-head budget of 2,048 entries, excluding prefill and setup costs; the missing Full-KV* points are out-of-memory runs, and Appendix D gives the full protocol.

Decode then performs dense paged GQA directly over the retained entries, without a mask or gather, and both cache storage and historical KV reads scale with $\sum_{h}B_{h}$ rather than the original context length, as reflected in Figure 5.
Figure 5, summarized in Section 4.5, reports aggregate batch decode throughput (token/s) on one NVIDIA H20 GPU for Qwen3-4B and Qwen3-8B.

abstract: Abstract: KV cache eviction must decide which entries carry information that the rest of the cache can no longer supply. A natural way to estimate this is a learnable gate: give each cached entry a gate on its attention weight and train the gate on the model’s own objective. The gate belongs inside the normalizing softmax, where suppressing one entry hands its mass to the others rather than discarding it. That same normalizer absorbs any per-query constant, so a constant gate cancels and reproduces the frozen model exactly. Trained on the language-modeling loss the gate stays near a constant score while its loss falls throughout: optimization succeeds, but a frozen backbone was fit for dense attention, so its loss prefers the no-op, and a near-constant score ranks nothing. The no-op is not a floor the gate improves from but what its objective asks for. A second obstacle survives once the gate moves, since the same gradient charges the gate for errors the frozen model already makes, which no reweighting of positions separates out. Much of the machinery in learnable eviction, from sparsity penalties to relaxations of the discrete decision, works around the first obstacle rather than removing it; both are removed by putting dense attention beyond the gate’s reach and making the dense model’s predictions its target. Under these two conditions capacity is never the missing ingredient: neither a larger scorer, nor explicit access to the past, nor a trainable backbone helps. The same holds for what eviction unavoidably discards, which is recovered by parameter-free centroids read inside the same softmax far better than by any memory read outside it, since the mass they must return is a share of that normalizer and available nowhere else. At 75% KV cache compression, this gate reaches 90.14 on RULER at 8K and 46.03 on LongBench with Qwen3-8B, 3.72 and 1.36 points below full-cache inference.

sections.body: The paper argues that KV eviction should keep entries that only the cache holds and drop those the rest of the cache can recover. This is query-independent redundancy rather than query relevance. A gate is trained inside the softmax on each entry's hidden state. The paper reports that naive training collapses to near-constant scores. The proposed IndexMem++ adds a recovery branch of parameter-free centroids inside the same softmax. At 75% compression, IndexMem++ reaches 90.14 on RULER at 8K with Qwen3-8B and 46.03 on LongBench, within 1.36 points of Full-KV. Section 4 gives the full comparison.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: Eviction should drop entries recoverable from the rest of the cache; the paper proposes an in-softmax gate with a recovery branch.

sections.body: Removing a cache entry must also remove its share of the normalizer. A gate applied after the softmax scales the value but leaves the other weights unchanged, so the suppressed mass is lost. A gate inside the softmax renormalizes over the gated entries. For binary gates this is exact attention over the retained set. The paper uses a per-key additive logit bias $\log g_j$ as the differentiable relaxation, because it does not depend on future query content. Query, key, value, and denominator gates are compared and found to have different effects on attention mass.
sections.heading: Attention mass and the eviction gate
sections.headline: A gate placed inside the softmax redistributes evicted mass to retained entries, while outer gates only scale values.

sections.body: The pilot uses Qwen3-0.6B on RULER at 8K with a budget of 2048 entries and 100 training steps per arm. The direct design, an MLP scorer trained with the language-modeling loss, reaches 4.33 against 70.01 for the dense model, because a constant score is a no-op inside the softmax. Protecting sinks and a local window, and requiring evictable entries to share a fixed mass, raises the score to 44.86. Distillation to the dense model's predictions gives 58.86, and retained-mass head budgets give 67.60. Unfreezing the backbone lowers eviction to 62.83 while Full-KV rises to 71.65, so the backbone stays frozen. Centroid recovery raises Math500 at 512 entries from 48.00 to 52.00 on Qwen3-0.6B.
sections.heading: Method
sections.headline: Naive training collapses to constant scores; fixed-mass competition, protected entries and distillation avoid that collapse.

sections.body: IndexMem++ is compared with SnapKV, KeyDiff, DMA, TrimKV, and KVpop on RULER. On math it is compared with R-KV, TriAttention, KVzap, Fast-KVzip, and Random Attention. Only the gate is trained, with the backbone frozen, on long documents. At 75% compression on RULER 8K with Qwen3-8B, IndexMem++ scores 90.14, against 80.26 for TrimKV and 72.71 for KVpop at the same ratio. On Math500 at a 512-entry budget, IndexMem++ scores 0.794 against 0.784 for Random Attention. On AIME25 at 2048 entries it scores 0.600 against 0.388. Decode throughput at batch size 32 drops about 28% from 8K to 256K input. Math pass@1 is estimated from two or eight rollouts per problem.
sections.heading: Experiments
sections.headline: At 75% compression IndexMem++ reaches 90.14 on RULER 8K with Qwen3-8B, the highest of the compared methods.

sections.body: Learnable eviction methods such as TrimKV, DMC, DMS, SP-KV, Locret, and Attention-Gate score entries with a lightweight scorer. The paper groups these methods together under one design. It also studies the scorer, normalization and budget, supervision, and head allocation. For recovery, prior work reads a summary either as a residual added to the attention output, with a gain learned outside the softmax, or as extra participants that compete for mass inside the softmax. The paper argues that this readout choice matters more than the capacity of the summary.
sections.heading: Related work
sections.headline: Prior learnable eviction gates use similar scorers, while recovery methods differ in whether the summary shares the softmax.

sections.body: A gate trained on the model's own loss prefers keeping everything, so it returns constant scores. The question becomes answerable when evictable entries compete for a fixed gate mass and the gate matches the dense model's predictions rather than the next token. Per-head budget is read from the retained attention mass. Some information is still lost. The paper concludes that a small memory should be read through the same softmax as the cache it supplements, rather than building a larger memory.
sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.headline: A gate trained on the model's own loss keeps everything; fixed-mass competition, dense-model distillation and softmax readout fix this.

sections.body: The gate is trained on dense or teacher-forced prefixes but applied to a cache that its own earlier decisions have compressed. The paper proposes on-policy distillation, with prefixes generated under hard eviction, to match the states seen at inference. The section also has an AI use statement, an ethics statement noting that compression can drop evidence the uncompressed model would use, and a reproducibility statement that points to appendices for the kernels, training recipe, and protocols. The paper states that it releases no new dataset or model.
sections.heading: Future work
sections.headline: Future work proposes on-policy distillation, since the gate is trained on dense prefixes but applied to compressed caches.

sections.body: The appendix reviews training-free eviction, sparse attention, and gate placements in attention, with a table of gate locations and a table of additive bias families. It also gives the trace analysis protocol. Overlap with a recency window is 52.50% on AIME25 and 48.35% on SWE, so about half of the retained entries lie outside it. In free generation on AIME25, IndexMem++ reaches a pass@1 of 0.592, against 0.121 for the recency policy and 0.654 for Full-KV.
sections.heading: Appendix
sections.headline: The appendix covers related work, gate placements, additive biases, and retention analyses on long agent and math reasoning traces.
